articles.title: Manchester City confirm appeal lodged against guilty verdict
articles.summary: The club's statement says the ruling contains "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".
articles.body:
Manchester City have confirmed they have lodged an appeal after an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

In a short statement, the club said the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Asserting its innocence, the club added it had filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions" on Thursday evening.

Earlier on Friday, the Football Association said the verdict against City has "significant implications for the integrity of the game".

In a statement, English football's governing body added: "We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate."

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

"As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage," the FA added.

"We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely."

The overarching powers the FA has could see the governing body launch its own investigation into the matter with the threat of further sanctions.

Sources told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

What does Man City guilty verdict mean for their squad?

Punish Man City this season, say other club chiefs

Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks

Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The findings have prompted the Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), to ask whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the cross-party group of MPs, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates , external which claims City failed to pay as much as £12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to £24m.

Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions

The commission was made up of three people, each with many years' experience in the legal field.

The appeal will now be heard in private by a new, three-person independent commission panel, each with a similar expert background in law.

One section of the Premier League regulations says that an appeal hearing should conclude within 12 weeks of it being heard, and a decision communicated within 30 days of that.

Twelve weeks from Thursday – when City say they lodged the appeal – would be 24 December.

But this timeframe can also be disapplied if deemed necessary, meaning it remains uncertain how long the process will actually take.

The relevant regulation was only added to the rule book this summer.

Previous precedent suggests that sanctions against City will only be imposed after a decision on the appeal, though this is not guaranteed.

There could therefore also be a second appeal later down the line, against any sanctions imposed on the club.

City will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.

This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.

Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.

City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".

The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.

articles.title: Manchester City charges: What does guilty verdict mean for players?
articles.summary: BBC Sport looks at how Manchester City's guilty verdict will affect their existing players' futures and the club's dealings in the transfer market.
articles.body:
So much has been said about Manchester City since it was revealed they had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 Premier League charges levelled at them.

On Tuesday, it was confirmed that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. The club has repeatedly denied guilt.

Their potential punishment has been debated, the future of the owners questioned and the feelings of the rest of the league - and wider football world - have been aired.

But so far there has been little focus on what it means for one crucial group.

Without definitive clarity on what sanctions the Premier League will impose, pending the appeal City have lodged , there is uncertainty over their ability to retain players, renew contracts, and make transfers - and whether any of the team have release clauses.

Put simply, will players want to join? Will current players want to stay?

BBC Sport has spoken to a number of sources in an attempt to understand how the recent judgement will impact City's dealings in the transfer market and how existing players may approach their futures with the prospect of losing Premier League status hanging over the club.

Man City confirm appeal against guilty verdict

Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions

The general train of thought is that any drop down the leagues for City will result in a mass exodus.

That players will, at the very least, consider their futures at Etihad Stadium in the event of demotion would be understandable.

The squad is brimming with international talent, many of whose profiles and personal sponsorship agreements benefit from plying their trade in the Premier League.

The reaction from current members of the City squad varies depending on who you speak to.

From the conversations BBC Sport have had with sources close to the first team, there is certainly a significant level of concern as to how they will be affected.

Given the scathing tone of the Premier League's statement on Tuesday, there is major scepticism from people close to the players that the forthcoming appeals will earn the club any reprieve.

But there are others who absolutely believe in City executives Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano's vows to prove the club's innocence.

For those players who decide they don't want to drop down the divisions, should it come to that, the process of leaving is unlikely to be straightforward.

Firstly there is the contract and the player registrations. City, regardless of each individual's view on whether they want to depart, have the right to demand transfer fees.

Given how much those players are worth in terms of wages and their general value in the market you'd imagine City are unlikely to accept being undercut.

That, as BBC Sport understands, the majority of players do not have relegation clauses in their contracts also plays into the club's hands.

But it is also understood that as a general rule the players' contracts are fully guaranteed, meaning they would not be required to take percentage pay cuts if they lose their top-flight status.

With one of the highest wage bills in the world, maintaining that level of salary expenditure, even for a club as financially capable as City, will become harder without Premier League-level income.

Parachute money could ease those concerns, although there are no guarantees that the club would be entitled to those payments if they are demoted.

With that in mind, City deciding to keep the squad completely intact should they move down the leagues appears unlikely.

Man City Q&A with Kieran Maguire & Dale Johnson

How amenable City are to selling players will be dependent on how bullish they are about it all.

Are they a distressed seller? Probably not. They still hold strong control of the situation regardless of how their players may feel.

It is unlikely the club will just simply roll over and let disillusioned players depart without suitable offers because, ultimately, they can ride the storm financially.

Players will have massive decisions to make too, not just in respect of leaving.

City are big payers, and other clubs may not be willing to meet similar wage demands.

"Some players want medals, all players want money," one agent said to BBC Sport.

In terms of potential contract renewals, the current uncertainty over what sanctions will be meted out provides a major element of risk.

Amending a contract retrospectively, say for example to include a relegation clause, generally cannot happen.

Any deals that include exit strategies for players if the club fall out of the Premier League would have to be negotiated as new contracts.

Players will likely want to wait for clarity on the sanctions before entering into contract discussions, adding a layer of difficulty for the club.

One way round persuading a player to renew would be to offer a significant financial incentive to re-sign to negate the risk of relegation.

But a number of agents who spoke to BBC Sport believe players will be advised to wait for clarity on the punishments before even considering opening talks.

Thankfully for City, only Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes, Marcus Bettinelli and Geronimo Rulli have contracts expiring in the next two summers, so that issue isn't as urgent as it could have been.

City's potential challenges with player contracts comes with Fifa preparing to introduce new rules that state every deal signed on 1 January, 2027 or after must include a release clause.

Guardiola backing Man City after guilty verdicts

Punish Man City this season, say other club chiefs

HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case

The looming punishment certainly complicates City's plans in the transfer market.

"This isn't the players' failing, it's on the club. Potential new signings aren't even in the building and joining City without knowing what the punishment would be represents an undeniable risk, so any new contracts would have to have indemnities," said one leading agent.

It was acknowledged that writing eventualities into new registrations is very difficult, though City players do have release clauses in their deals should the club enter into administration.

Until a post-appeal verdict over sanctions is made, making new signings will certainly become more complicated, though it is still likely they will be able to attract big players as they still have the financial muscle to do so.

For example, one potential method of persuading a player to join would be to offer them a contract on big money with no pay decreases if the club are relegated, and then include a fixed fee release clause if City don't return to the top flight within a set period.

If sanctions ensure relegation and include further points deductions that stretch over multiple seasons, attracting top players will of course be harder.

City could make a wage package hard to resist for elite players, but it seems inconceivable that a footballer of that ilk would join with demotion a possibility as there are likely to be other top options elsewhere.

The same logic can be applied to the retention of their current squad.

There is almost certainly going to be interest in their top players from other elite clubs across Europe. It will be very difficult for City to keep that level of player in the coming months and years while the saga plays out.

So with all that said, particularly if relegation is confirmed, City will have to rebuild their squad to some extent, though the prospect of a transfer embargo as one of the sanctions would prevent them from making any signings at all.

Such a rebuild may include the promotion of some of the club's best academy players, who stand to benefit if the first-team squad disbands.

When Chelsea were placed under a transfer embargo in 2019, the likes of Mason Mount, Tammy Abraham, Fikayo Tomori, Billy Gilmour and Callum Hudson-Odoi all emerged as senior players.

And while City may look to rebuild with a profile of player they believe will be adept at being successful in the EFL, you will likely see a number of their younger players fast-tracked.

With that said, a number of clubs are already working on seeing if they can capitalise on the current uncertainty by luring City's best academy talent.

articles.title: Ian Holloway: Swindon boss labels himself 'dead man walking' unless form changes
articles.summary: Swindon manager Ian Holloway calls himself a "dead man walking" if the team's form does not turn around.
articles.body:
Swindon manager Ian Holloway has described himself as a "dead man walking" if the club's form does not turn around.

The Robins are 12th in the League Two table with three victories out of eight league games this season and winless in their past three.

Holloway, who took over almost two years ago, said the team needs more backing with 13 players out injured, which equates to almost half of the squad.

"Dead. Man. Walking. That's how it feels, but deep down I know a lot more than that, don't I?" Holloway told BBC Radio Wiltshire.

"I know what I've done, I know where I am, I know the problems I've got here, I've tried to explain them openly and honestly to everybody."

Swindon travel to Rochdale on Saturday without any wins on the road this season and Holloway said the players "need some help".

"For them to have a chance, boy oh boy, don't we need something to go right immediately," he said.

"If it doesn't I'll be cheering them on and then I'm not sure how many more will. I believe they need some help right now and that's what I'm trying to do.

"I have to stand up for what I think my team needs, deserves and should have anyway. I'm sorry we haven't won every game. We've got 11 points on the board, we wanted a lot more. We've got 10 at home, one away and the away form needs to change."

'Never seen' injury crisis like this before

Holloway added he has "never seen" an injury crisis like the one the club is enduring at the moment.

They travel to Rochdale with captain Ollie Clarke, Matty Virtue and Paul Glatzel the latest to join the injured list.

"Ollie might not be able to play, Matty's not fit and Glatzel's had some stuff drawn off his knee so he's out as well," Holloway said.

Swindon are already without Joe Snowdon, Ryan Tafazolli, Ollie Palmer, Gavin Kilkenny, Jaylan Pearman, Harry Smith and Fletcher Holman while Mitch Clark is still serving a suspension after being sent off against York and Sam Inwood is away on international duty.

"I've [said] Louis [Millard] is fit - that's 13 out if Louis is not fit. He trained yesterday and he looked fit but his shoulder is still very sore. If he's not fit, then we've only got 15," Holloway said.

Midfielder Ben Middlemass is facing a lengthy spell on the sidelines and will need surgery on a cartilage issue, with Holloway expecting him to be out for a minimum of eight weeks, which he said "could be 20 weeks".

The nature of full-back Joel McGregor's injury is unknown as he is still to see a specialist.

With many players expected to be out long-term, Holloway said it is putting undue pressure on those still within the playing squad.

"This injury crisis - and it is a crisis - [I've] never seen anything like it because the nature of their injuries is going to make it hard for them to get back, as they weren't fit anyway because they've missed pre-season," he said.

"Now the ones that we did have who were vulnerable, we're having to ask too much from them."

articles.title: Craig Bellamy: Was long-awaited win a turning point for Wales boss?
articles.summary: Has the impressive 2-1 victory over Norway changed the mood music for Wales and restored fans confidence in head coach Craig Bellamy?
articles.body:
And perhaps the end of Craig Bellamy's summer of discontent.

The significance of the victory over Norway was not lost on the Wales head coach.

After all, goals from Neco Williams and Dan James – as well as shutting out Erling Haaland – delivered not only Wales' first win in seven games, but their first ever in Nations League A.

Indeed, this was only the second time Wales have beaten a side ranked higher than them in a competitive fixture since reaching the semi-finals of Euro 2016.

And even if it wasn't obvious at the final whistle as he calmly shook hands with Stale Solbakken and his staff, Bellamy knew it too.

From March's disappointment over missing out on the World Cup, to June's dalliance with Burnley, it has been a testing time for a head coach still trying to make his mark with his country.

Those summer clouds that had darkened the atmosphere among fans had lingered into the start of this Nations League campaign. Stormier still after the manner of defeat in Denmark.

But, on a clear night in Cardiff, the evening's skies ended up filled only with the sound of the national anthem serenading a re-energised national side's efforts.

A song to signal a turning point? Perhaps, but it was certainly in contrast to the mood music just a few hours before kick-off.

Just as they had done on the night World Cup dreams were ended on penalties by Bosnia-Herzegovina, prior to Thursday's game fans gathered at the Canopi venue in the shadow of the Principality Stadium where – all being well – Wales will kick-off a home European Championships in less than two years time.

That prospect was not the topic of conversation of the Red Wall members present, though, with many instead deep in discussion of where and why things seemed to have gone wrong under Bellamy.

From going unbeaten in his opening nine games with a refreshing brand of football, the consensus was things had gone flat and that the head coach was bearing the brunt of it.

"I think people were down on him after Bosnia, the way the game panned out and seeing mistakes we made on the night we'd made earlier in the campaign," said Ryan March, fan and editor of Alternative Wales, the fanzine that had organised the pre-match meet.

"He didn't really come out and say he'd made an error, and then when the Burnley thing happened, perhaps people thought it might be good for a change and we could move on.

"When it didn't, I expected a reaction – and we haven't had it."

Bellamy speaks out over criticism after Norway win

Although never a yardstick to always take seriously, the reaction on social media has been more extreme. In real life, the opinion was less that Bellamy had to go, but he had to be better.

The promise and possibilities offered from Bellamy's exciting opening to life as head coach were seen as having petered out.

"Are we a better side than we were at the end of his first year in charge? I don't think we are," added March.

"We have less of a style, less of an identity, and we've not been better than the sum of our parts, which the best Welsh sides always tend to be."

It was something Bellamy had addressed and admitted in his press conference prior to the game, accepting he deserved scrutiny.

"We need to improve; I need to improve," he had said.

It was a revealing piece of humility, especially given some supporters suggested a sense of being tired of Wales – and their head coach – "talking a good game".

A mile down the road in the Canton suburb of the Welsh capital, feelings were not dissimilar - although some long-standing fans reminded others of a history of impatience among Wales fans with their manager, scolding some supporters' reaction in Copenhagen.

And there were plenty of caveats being offered.

A four-game window without first-choice goalkeeper Karl Darlow, a first-choice centre-back in Joe Rodon and a go-to attacking threat in Harry Wilson was accepted as a tough hand to have been dealt, likewise the calibre of opposition.

Instead of Premier League regulars, League One options have to be turned to at times.

Then there were the arguably unfair expectation levels following recent success in qualifying for major tournaments, as well as those set publicly by Bellamy himself when he told supporters to no longer accept being "little old Wales."

A group of fans, who point out the previous dark days following the national team, mentioned all of the above, but still questioned tactics, game-management and the 'coach-speak' of Bellamy and whether there may be another club offer to tempt him on the horizon.

And then they all chuckled in admission when another suggests the mood will change in an instant with victory over a side ranked 19th in the world and boasting hundred-million pound talents.

And yet it was the performance perhaps more than the result that appeared to win fans over again and reset the relationship between supporter and head coach.

"If they wanted to turn, that was their chance," Bellamy said on S4C of the crowd response to Oscar Bobb's opener after 11 minutes in what was Wales' first home game since those Burnley links. "But they didn't, they drove players on."

Indeed, there had been only a Red Walled-willingness for Wales - and Bellamy - to be better throughout the 90 minutes, the noise lifting as Haaland remained contained and the hosts continued to move forward. They liked what they saw. Action, not words.

Bellamy admitted to having an "identity meeting" with players to try and re-establish what had been the hallmarks of his initial time in charge. It evidently did the trick given the way the tempo and aggression returned.

On the ball there was plenty to please the eye, not to mention the resilience to close a game out – a key criticism of that World Cup campaign.

One win is only one win, but there were red-shirted signs of redemption, from Liam Cullen's performance - a player Bellamy has been criticised for selecting over others - to Neco Williams' free-kick following a difficult night in Denmark.

But suddenly the Nations League campaign has new life and the chance of remaining in the top tier, and maybe even a seeding boost for those Euro 2028 qualifiers.

"It felt more like what we saw at the start under Craig," said former Wales midfielder Joe Ledley.

"I think people have wanted to see it back but they saw it here. Fans don't always have patience, decision-makers don't always have patience so I think everyone knew we needed to see a result – but we also saw the performance and things we've not seen for a while. That's a Craig Bellamy side."

So instead of breaking point, was this a turning point?

"I hope so," said Robert Earnshaw, another former Wales teammate of Bellamy and now part of the Match of the Day Wales team with Ledley.

"Craig needed it, the team needed it, I think the whole nation needed it," said Earnshaw.

"Our levels dropped after the disappointment of the World Cup and it was about how could we bounce back - and here we felt that energy and excitement again.

"They had to give the crowd things to be cheerful about, because they were missing that for a while. Against Denmark we were miles away from what we've seen.

And – although the next test fast approaches against Denmark in Cardiff on Sunday - maybe it was also a line drawn.

articles.title: De la Barrera zanja el asunto: "Loiodice jugará en el centro del campo"
articles.standfirst: Reconoce que los ajustes en la presión, y no el francés, fueran la causa de los goles del Éibar
articles.summary: Reconoce que los ajustes en la presión, y no el francés, fueran la causa de los goles del Éibar
articles.body: Con naturalidad y de manera pedagógicas. Así ha explicado Rubén de la Barrera las causas y las consecuencias de los resultados de su equipo en las últimas jornadas. Lejos de sentirse atacado, el técnico de Las Palmas ha expuesto los motivos de la mala racha. Uno de esos motivos es la fragilidad que está demostrando el equipo en los balones a la espalda, exculpando a Loiodice, que ha tenido que jugar como lateral zurdo: "¿Qué grado de responsabilidad tiene Enzo en los goles? Nada. La responsabilidad fue de nuestra presión, que no está bien hecha". Reconoce, además, que el francés jugará, pero "en centro del campo". La posición de lateral izquierdo queda en el aire. Eso sí, el que tiene más posibilidades de entrar es Andrés Rodríguez posiblemente como defensa central: "Tenemos que convivir con ausencias y eso son oportunidades para otros, que están condicionadas por el tipo de partido que tenemos". El gallego podría ampararse en la cantidad de bajas que tiene. También en una desajustada confección de plantilla. Sin embargo, el entrenador no ha querido parapetarse en ese tipo de aspectos: "No me considero víctima de nada. Soy entrenador, y mi labor es hacer lo que está en mi mano para que esto vaya bien", ha sentenciado. También ha sido cuestionado por Jesé. El entrenador ha salido a la defensa de su delantero: "La experiencia le ha permitido ganar en compresión y conocimiento del juego. Él defiende, y defender no es correr como un loco, es hacerlo con inteligencia. Jesé es francamente inteligente. Decir Jesé no está comprometido en el momento defensivo es faltar a la verdad".

articles.title: B/R Experts' October Bold Predictions for 2026 CFB Season
articles.summary: Being bold never gets old.
articles.body:
We're a month-plus into the college football season. Teams have shown their true colors. Some are off to fast starts, while others have disappointed.

The only predictable thing in college football is that it's going to be unpredictable, so why not go out on shaky limbs this early? Right now, almost anything can still happen, right?

The College Football Playoff picture is a little clearer than it was at the start of the year. The top players are separating themselves from the field. So, let's get crazy.

It's no fun to predict Texas or Georgia wins the Natty, or Darian Mensah hoists the Heisman Trophy, because those things are expected at the moment. Some things, though, really make you go, "Whoa."

B/R Experts David Kenyon, Adam Kramer, Joel Reuter and Brad Shepard have your wild and wacky right here. Let's get bold, shall we?

Kenyon: Oklahoma Falls Short of Bowl Eligibility

Brent Venables is not on the hot seat. His recently signed two-year extension prevents us from having that conversation.

Check the mood around Oklahoma, however, and you would probably think otherwise. I'm not here to say that's wrong, either. The offense has been nothing short of an absolute disaster this season, falling short of 300 yards in three straight games against Michigan, New Mexico and Georgia.

John Mateer, once a prized transfer QB, has dealt with serious turnover issues that aren't simply a product of bad luck. He's making poor decisions downfield and not protecting the ball as a runner. The staff even considered benching him during the UGA loss. Compounding the problem is OU's offensive line, which isn't blocking much of anything. So far, the Sooners are 98th in sacks allowed, 111th in tackles for loss allowed and a horrendous 134th—out of 138 teams nationally—in yards per carry.

Given what's left on the schedule, the 2-2 Sooners may struggle to even hit bowl eligibility. The remaining slate includes six AP Top 25 teams, including No. 1 Texas, No. 8 Florida and No. 9 Ole Miss. Unless OU springs an upset in one of those contests, it'll need a 4-1 finish to reach six wins.

Maybe that happens. But there isn't much evidence to support it right now.

Kramer: UCLA Makes the College Football Playoff

Through four games, UCLA has looked the part. While the Bruins haven't played a ranked opponent yet, they've played twice on the road and looked downright dominant at times. They've also played three Power Four teams, which is more than most can say.

Yes, Bob Chesney looks like one of the next great coaches in college football. He's taken a program that seemed adrift and brought it immediate life. We'd go so far as to say the whole thing looks Indiana Light right now.

Here's the part with UCLA that is really intriguing: the schedule.

Sure, the Bruins play at Oregon. They also play at Michigan and close out with USC. But the rest of the games look extremely manageable. It wouldn't be surprising one bit to see this team flirt with a two-loss season.

At the very least, that would put UCLA in contention. Given where this season started, what a moment it would be.

Reuter: Malachi Toney and Jeremiah Smith Are Both Heisman Trophy Finalists

In the 91 years the Heisman Trophy has been awarded, there has never been a season where two wide receivers finished in the top five in balloting, so having them occupy two seats as finalists in New York would be uncharted territory.

Ohio State star Jeremiah Smith (33 catches, 618 yards, 7 TD) is the current odds favorite entering Week 5, followed by Miami quarterback Darian Mensah. However, his top target Malachi Toney (34 catches, 564 yards, 6 TD) is also on the board as a top-10 candidate. There's a case to be made for him overtaking his teammate.

The share of production Smith has provided (51.2% of team receiving yards, 23.3% of team points) isn't as far ahead of Toney's impact (46.6% of team receiving yards, 17.6% of team points) as you might think. So if Smith is the leading candidate over Julian Sayin, the same should apply to Miami's candidates.

Both teams are also part of the College Football Playoff conversation and will remain in the national spotlight, but Toney has a significantly easier road ahead. Miami's only remaining currently ranked opponent is Notre Dame, while Ohio State still faces Iowa, Indiana, USC and Oregon.

B/R's Latest Heisman Trophy Odds and Rankings 🔢

As a Florida believer, I thought about going bold with a Gators pick, but given that they're in the top 10, that didn't quite fit the "bold" bill. So, let's head west instead.

Stillwater, Oklahoma, is experiencing an unexpected resurgence of first-year coach Eric Morris' Oklahoma State Cowboys. They are 3-1 and just whipped West Virginia in Morgantown.

A successful season seemed a stretch following a 24-10 season-opening loss to Tulsa, but OSU stunned Oregon 39-31 in Week 2 and hasn't looked back.

This isn't fool's gold. The tandem of QB Drew Mestemaker and RB Caleb Hawkins is elite, proving they can do it on any stage. Their familiarity with Morris' high-octane attack is turning viewers who see them play into believers.

Massive games at Houston (October 17) and at home against Texas Tech (November 14) loom, but split those and run the table, and the Cowboys are likely in the Big 12 championship game. This is a team with the dangerous combination of youth, belief and talent in a wide-open conference.

I like the Cowboys' path to shocking the nation.

articles.title: Women's Super League live on Sky this weekend: Man City to hand further punishment to Renee Slegers and Arsenal?
articles.summary: Man City host under-fire Arsenal in this weekend's showpiece game with the chance to extend their lead at the top of the Women's Super League; watch all SIX WSL games live on Sky Sports this Sunday from 2pm; watch Man City vs Arsenal at 4.30pm
articles.body:
Man City could stick the boot in on Slegers

Man City vs Arsenal - Sunday, kick-off 4.30pm, live on Sky Sports

While the turmoil engulfing Manchester City Football Club rumbles on in the background of M11, I have no doubt Andree Jeglertz will insist nothing changes for his reigning champs. And why should it? City are thriving under him, top of the WSL, unbeaten since April.

Arsenal, meanwhile, are stuck in a revolving rut. Things have gone stale under Renee Slegers, who needs a big result to breathe some life into a tenure that is increasingly gathering unwanted attention. The Gunners are winless in each of their last three league outings and Slegers has come in for criticism after her side blew a two-goal lead in Paris to draw 2-2 midweek.

Subjectively, I'm in the camp that defeat on Sunday ends their title race. The gap to City as leaders would already be 10 points and that deficit is rarely surmountable. It's on Arsenal to approach the game with the kind of authority that, so far, has been absent from most of their disjointed performances. They must show up.

City are unlikely to take pity; if they sense even a flicker of vulnerability, they will go for the kill.

Man Utd vs Liverpool - Saturday, kick-off 1.30pm

Man Utd remain on a voyage of discovery under Eva Olid. What is their style of play? How much is realistically achievable this season? Is evolution as a club even possible in the current climate? There is limited evidence from which to draw conclusions at this early stage.

But I admired their endeavour in victory over West Ham last weekend, Olid's first in the WSL. Her side carried equal threat from open play and set-pieces, and scored two well-worked goals. The Spaniard's desire to develop an aggressive, pressing team was far more detectable - but it's clearly a work in progress.

Despite ranking among the sides who have amassed the fewest shots and one of the lowest accumulated xG values, they also have the best conversion rate in the WSL. That tells me they are being smart with the rare moments they get, but have to be better at generating more sustained attacking intent in order to improve creatively.

Summer signing Andrea Medina has carried the torch so far, but I also liked what I saw from Ella Toone last week - playing with an axe to grind after her latest England snub.

Tottenham vs London City Lionesses - Sunday, kick-off 2pm, live on Sky Sports

This is a game that fascinates me. Since the start of April, only Chelsea and Man City have won more points per game than Tottenham's 2.4. London City are close behind with 2.1. Form meets form.

These are the kinds of close-run contests that will define the next stage of development for two sides who have designs on breaking the establishment. Only once have Spurs amassed more points after four played. They are demonstrating new levels of tactical variety with the craft and consistency of their attacking output.

It's difficult not to get overexcited, but Martin Ho is a realist. He will know this weekend is big.

I expect London City captain Alexia Putellas to thrive in phases of the game that Spurs leave themselves open. If you give an elite playmaker space to exploit, better believe she will find the gaps that hurt you most.

Her strike in victory over Brighton last week signals she is beginning to settle into new surroundings and that has the power to create a domino effect. The Spaniard has ended on the winning side in 129 of the last 130 league games she has scored in.

Has Chelsea's ruthlessness finally returned?

West Ham vs Chelsea - Sunday, kick-off 2pm, live on Sky Sports

Chelsea have conceded just once in the WSL this season - the fewest of any side. That is the kind of belligerence title charges are built on.

After a slightly stuttering start, Sonia Bompastor's side have clicked into gear and are ticking games off with an efficiency that reminds me of eras gone by. My pre-season judgement that they remain light on firepower has been mitigated somewhat by the step up from other departments.

Excluding own goals, Chelsea boast the joint-most goalscorers in the division (8). Such a spread not only gives them threat from all over the pitch but also makes them hard to predict, with constant variation in movement and game pace.

Bompastor has been bullish in her pursuit of the ruthless edge that appeared to be lost when Emma Hayes departed. Recent results suggest she is getting closer to finding it.

Aston Villa vs Crystal Palace - Sunday, kick-off 2pm, live on Sky Sports

Aston Villa are winless in each of their last eight WSL outings, which goes some way to explaining why Natalia Arroyo lost her job this week - the first managerial casualty of the season. I saw flashes of exciting, progressive play under the Spanish coach but results were far too erratic to allow time for such a style to properly develop.

Villa also lost top-scorer Kirsty Hanson to Tottenham in the summer and that probably gives you a good indication of where they are at in the competitive food chain.

Both Villa and Sunday's opponents Crystal Palace have already shipped a league-high 10 goals each this term, facing a combined 223 shots against. The only area of focus for Villa's interim boss Brian Sorensen is surely to address that shortfall.

Brighton vs Charlton - Sunday, kick-off 2pm, live on Sky Sports

Charlton are the only team without a point this season, managing just two shots on target and one solitary goal. They badly need something to fall their way, and Brighton might just be the obliging hosts their predicament could exploit.

Brighton are winless in seven in the WSL and are only two points better off in the standings. Arturo Ruiz has not yet had the time he needs to get his ideas across after taking over from Dario Vidosic so late in the day. He did not get the benefit of a pre-season to prune this inherited squad. Charlton should look for any opportunity to profit.

Everton vs Birmingham City - Sunday, kick-off 2pm, live on Sky Sports

A weird quirk of this season is that Everton have won two games without scoring a single goal themselves. 360 minutes have passed without a Toffees player finding the net in the top flight, benefiting from two own goals to take six points from 12. It's a solid return but clearly they need to start producing goals of their own volition to build further.

Someone who is not struggling in front of goal is Birmingham City's Oceane Hurtre. The 22-year-old has scored four already and can be the difference as the Blues chase their first win since returning to the WSL.

This Sunday sees SIX games broadcast live across Sky Sports channels, culminating in a huge top-of-the-table clash between Manchester City and Arsenal at 4.30pm.

You can also follow action from every game across our dedicated digital coverage, with in-game clips and free-to-watch highlights.

articles.title: El informe técnico de FIFA ya es una realidad: así ha cambiado el fútbol tras el Mundial
articles.standfirst: El Grupo de Estudio Técnico de la FIFA y el Departamento de Perspectivas del Rendimiento Futbolístico de la FIFA analizaron los 104 partidos del Mundial de este año
articles.summary: El Grupo de Estudio Técnico de la FIFA y el Departamento de Perspectivas del Rendimiento Futbolístico de la FIFA analizaron los 104 partidos del Mundial de este año
articles.body: Varios meses después de la celebración en Nueva Jersey de la final del Mundial 2026 que coronó a España con su segunda estrella, la FIFA ha publicado un informe muy completo de dicha Copa del Mundo. El análisis ofrece perspectivas inéditas sobre cómo las mejores selecciones nacionales y los mejores jugadores del planeta están definiendo el fútbol actual. El informe, elaborado por el Grupo de Estudio Técnico de la FIFA (GET) y el Departamento de Perspectivas del Rendimiento Futbolístico de la FIFA, se basa en las conclusiones extraídas de los 104 partidos del torneo. Las conclusiones principales, expuestas a continuación, destacan innovaciones tácticas, la evolución de las funciones de los jugadores y planteamientos novedosos para ganar partidos. "La Copa Mundial de la FIFA representa la máxima expresión del fútbol. Es una ocasión única que congrega a los mejores jugadores, seleccionadores y culturas futbolísticas de todo el planeta, y en la que cada uno de ellos aporta sus propias ideas, identidades y maneras de jugar", declaró Arsène Wenger, FIFA Chief of Global Football Development. "Para quienes nos encargamos de interpretar y desarrollar el fútbol, el Mundial nos brinda una oportunidad extraordinaria de observar el juego, aprender de él y plantearnos hacia dónde se dirige", añadió. El informe examina el juego en todas sus fases: desde cómo los equipos elaboraron los ataques y subieron el balón por el campo hasta cómo presionaron, defendieron y reaccionaron a los cambios de posesión. Estos son algunos de los temas principales: • Elaboración del juego con una defensa de tres: las distintas estructuras que emplearon los equipos que jugaban con una defensa de tres y cómo esta disposición les permitió elaborar las jugadas. • Intercambios de posiciones en las bandas: utilización de este recurso por parte de los equipos para generar espacios y desestabilizar la estructura defensiva rival. • Utilización de los carriles interiores: aprovechamiento por parte de los equipos de los espacios entre el carril central y lateral para avanzar y generar peligro. • Progresión mediante jugadores específicos: los jugadores y las funciones que resultaron fundamentales para subir el balón entre las estructuras defensivas del adversario. • Presión alta: cuándo y cómo los equipos aplicaron una presión alta y las oportunidades que se generaron cuando recuperaron el balón gracias a ella. • Presión tras pérdida: las respuestas de los equipos nada más perder el balón y su capacidad para recuperarlo o evitar las transiciones del adversario. • Bloques defensivos: de qué manera se organizaron los equipos en las fases sin posesión, y cómo protegieron los espacios más importantes y adaptaron sus estructuras defensivas. • Transiciones ofensivas: aprovechamiento por parte de los equipos de los instantes posteriores a una recuperación del balón y qué elementos contribuyeron a que las transiciones fueran fructíferas. • Evolución del rol de los guardametas: la función cada vez más influyente de los porteros cuando su equipo tiene la posesión, su posicionamiento en distintas fases del juego y las principales tendencias que han surgido en este torneo. El análisis del torneo, un documento de más de 500 páginas, se puede consultar ya en el Centro de Capacitación de la FIFA, de manera que entrenadores, analistas, jugadores y otros grupos de interés del fútbol tienen a su alcance información muy detallada. "Este informe engloba todo lo que observamos en la Copa Mundial de la FIFA 2026 y las tendencias técnicas y tácticas que marcan una competición. Y lo que es más importante: espero que dé pie a que entrenadores, jugadores y cualquier persona que participe en el desarrollo del fútbol cuestione estas observaciones, las debata y aprenda de ellas. La Copa Mundial de la FIFA nos muestra el fútbol en todo su esplendor, pero su verdadera trascendencia no radica solo en disfrutar con lo que vemos, sino en utilizar lo que hemos aprendido para ayudar a forjar su desarrollo", concluyó Wenger.

articles.title: Los ingresos comerciales del Manchester City se estancaron al empezar la investigación
articles.standfirst: Según un informe del diario británico 'The Times'
articles.summary: Según un informe del diario británico 'The Times'
articles.body: Los ingresos comerciales del Manchester City se estancaron en 2018, el mismo año en el que comenzó la investigación de la Premier League que ha terminado declarando culpable al club inglés de más de un centenar de irregularidades financieras. Según un informe del diario británico "The Times", el crecimiento comercial del Manchester City entre 2018 y 2025 (el último año del que se tienen datos), fue de un 46 %, de 232 millones (270 millones de euros) a 340 millones (400 millones de euros), un porcentaje que contrasta con el del Liverpool que duplicó sus ingresos un 110 %, de 154 millones a 323, y el Arsenal, que incrementó un 146 % de 107 millones a 263 millones. Desde 2008 -año en el que Abu Dabi compró el club- a 2025, el City vio cómo sus ingresos comerciales aumentaron de 25 millones a 340 millones. Al City se le ha declarado culpable de inflar sus cuentas a través de patrocinios adulterados con empresas que estaban bajo el mismo paraguas que el club, Emiratos Árabes Unidos. Los contratos comerciales que el City posee en estos momentos son 13,5 veces más valiosos que los que tenían en 2008 cuando se produjo la compra por parte del fondo de inversión de Abu Dabi. "The Times" apunta que LaLiga española manifestó en 2017 que los ingresos comerciales del City estaba muy por encima de lo que era normal y apuntó a los acuerdos que el club tenía con Emiratos Árabes Unidos. Según lo expuesto en la investigación y el veredicto de la Premier League y la comisión independiente que ha llevado el caso, el City infló sus presupuestos durante casi una década, desde 2009 a 2018, resultando en una adulteración de sus cuentas de más de 1.000 millones de euros. Durante este tiempo, el conjunto inglés amasó ocho títulos, incluyendo tres Premier League.

articles.title: Ryan Lowe interview: Wigan Athletic tenure, Preston North End departure and what's next
articles.summary: Ryan Lowe discusses his time at recent clubs Wigan Athletic and Preston North End, as well as what's next for the manager. Listen to the full interview on the Sky Sports Essential EFL podcast
articles.body:
In truth, the fact that it took Ryan Lowe until his fourth managerial role to get the chop is pretty astonishing in modern-day football.

He had enjoyed League Two promotion with Bury and Plymouth Argyle, before seasons at Preston where he feels they punched well above their weight in the Championship.

"It was a tough gig," Lowe told the Sky Sports Essential EFL podcast . "The first year, in 2024/25, we wanted to try and consolidate and stay in the division. We got 13 points from the first 11 or 12 games, but the remit was to stay in the division. We'd done that comfortably.

"The following year, we needed to try and kick on and we felt that we'd have a budget to compete. But the budgets were benchmarked from two years ago and stuff, so it was really difficult.

"We missed out on a lot of players because we couldn't compete with certain clubs. They were bigger and had better players than we were able to get.

"We had a good start to the season, really. We were doing OK, and then we lost Ryan Trevitt, who was a big, influential player for us. We built the team around him because he was very creative and everything.

"We had a few injuries and a few KPIs went against us, but that's not making excuses. There was a lot of stuff that I could have done better with and I know that, but so could a lot of other people who were there with me.

"It was tough. When you're being sacked, that was my first sacking and hopefully it's my last. But I understood it. The results weren't great. The performances were okay, the data was okay. We were still creating and whatnot, but we weren't clinical enough in front of goal."

Before Wigan, Lowe was at Preston. Punching above their weight in the Championship, he led them to two top-half finishes in his full seasons in charge.

He is full of belief that the relative struggles of the club since have shown what an impressive job he did there. His successor, Paul Heckingbottom, was sacked last month.

"The year I left, Hecky survived the last day of the season to stay in the Championship. Last season he finished 14th," Lowe continued. "He's a fantastic football manager and he ends up losing his job.

"Other people will question the style of play and what type of football you're playing. But what I chose and what I learned in the Championship, again from managers who we'd come up against, was how to adapt.

"I know deep down I did a good job there. That doesn't matter to anyone else, just for me and my own personal belief that I know I can do that. I'm a good manager in terms of overachieving on budgets.

"I don't think you can just go to places and say, 'I can go toe to toe with all Norwich's footballers.' We went to Norwich one year and played five at the back, 5-4-1, and nearly won. We drew 0-0, but it was a good point away from home."

One thing he does rue, however, is leaving Preston the way he did. Lowe knows he needed to go, but to do it after just one game of the 2024/25 season wasn't the right time.

"I do regret leaving after one game," he admitted. "But what I had to do was protect myself and my family at that time.

"Pre-season, I did contemplate it and I had a good chat with [chairman] Peter Ridsdale. There was a statement that went out at the end of that season before pre-season saying that it wasn't good enough for where we finished and the results weren't great.

"We played Sheffield United [on opening day] and lost 2-0. The two goals we conceded were very sloppy. I couldn't sleep at all that night and I was thinking, can I take it any further? Can I do justice for the club? They're paying me a lot of money to do this job and am I really giving the fans what they want? Am I really giving the footballers what they want?

"We sat down and had a gentleman's agreement. They didn't actually want me to leave, but I just felt at that time I wasn't advised very well on that side of it, if I'm being honest.

"My gut instinct was saying, just do it, do it, do it. I should have really waited. I should have given it the next few games. If I had been sacked, I would have been sacked. It wouldn't have really mattered anyway.

"I just felt that I'd taken it as far as I could take it. I didn't think we could get to the next level with the budgets, the squad and everything around it.

"Sadly, it's been proved right by where they've finished over the past few seasons. The only regret was doing it one game in."

He is keen on a return to football, and wants a project rather than a firefighting job. Something he has turned down in the past.

Even at Wigan, he was given a three-and-a-half year deal, before being sacked after less than 12 months.

"Wherever I go next, they will be getting the best version of Ryan Lowe because I'm disappointed with what happened," he said. "You don't want to be a firefighter, but I know you do sometimes have to go in somewhere and keep a side in the division.

"What I don't want to do is go into a club for 10 or 15 games with no longevity, just to get a few wins and then earn your contract. My CV speaks for itself.

"I'm 380 games in now as a manager, a lot of them in the Championship. I'm really keen to get back to a football club with a good ownership group and a good sporting director, and we're all on the same page."

articles.title: Kochen, una cesión que cotiza al alza
articles.standfirst: El meta es titular indiscutible en el Lyngby Boldklub y ha debutado con su selección
articles.summary: El meta es titular indiscutible en el Lyngby Boldklub y ha sido citado con su selección
articles.body: El overbooking en la portería del Barcelona durante el pasado verano obligó a Kochen a buscar una salida para continuar con su progresión. El guardameta, que la pasada temporada disputó 20 encuentros con el filial y llegó a entrar en 40 convocatorias con el primer equipo, optó por una cesión al Lyngby Boldklub. El objetivo era claro: encontrar la continuidad que difícilmente podía tener en el Spotify Camp Nou, acumular minutos y adquirir experiencia. La apuesta está dando sus frutos. Kochen se ha convertido en un fijo bajo los palos del conjunto danés. Ha disputado los nueve partidos de liga hasta el momento y ha completado todos ellos, una continuidad que le ha permitido consolidarse como una pieza importante del equipo. Su rendimiento tampoco ha pasado desapercibido para la selección. La regularidad que está mostrando en Dinamarca le ha abierto las puertas del combinado de Estados Unidos. Pochettino le incluyó en la convocatoria para este parón internacional y, además, le hizo debutar en el encuentro contra Perú. Kochen disputó 45 minutos con el combinado estadounidense, un nuevo paso en una temporada que está suponiendo un importante impulso para su carrera y puede convertirse en un punto de inflexión. La operación entre el Barcelona y el Lyngby se cerró mediante una cesión que incluye una opción de compra de 1,5 millones de euros. Para el club azulgrana, la fórmula permite que el guardameta continúe creciendo, y para Kochen representa la posibilidad de demostrar semana tras semana que está preparado para dar un paso adelante. Por ahora, los números avalan su evolución. Nueve partidos disputados, nueve titularidades y todos los minutos completados en la competición liguera reflejan el peso que tiene en su nuevo equipo. El guardameta está consiguiendo, por tanto, el principal objetivo que perseguía con su salida del Barcelona: jugar, acumular experiencia y crecer. Kochen se está revalorizando.

articles.title: Enzo Alves se presenta a la temporada
articles.standfirst: El hijo de Marcelo volverá el domingo a una convocatoria con el Juvenil A tras una lesión que le ha frenado en el inicio de la competición
articles.summary: El hijo de Marcelo volverá el domingo a una convocatoria con el Juvenil A tras una lesión que le ha frenado en el inicio de la competición
articles.body: Enzo Alves está de vuelta. El hijo de Marcelo volverá el domingo a una convocatoria con el Juvenil A del Real Madrid tras superar una lesión que le ha frenado en el inicio de la competición. El joven delantero de 17 años 'se presenta' a la temporada en octubre, un mes después de caer lesionado tras regresar de una concentración con la selección española sub 18. Un problema físico que ya está superado y tras varios días ejercitándose con normalidad con el primer juvenil blanco que dirige Álvaro López, ya está en condiciones de volver a jugar. Será el domingo ante el Rayo Alcobendas (17.00) cuando Enzo disfrute de sus primeros minutos oficiales de la temporada con el Real Madrid. Álvaro López recupera a un jugador capital para el equipo, en su condición de una de las grande joyas de La Fábrica, en un momento en el que se ha quedado sin delanteros: no cuenta con Yeremaiah (con la selección sub 18) ni con su actual Pichichi, Fran Santamaría, que será nuevamente convocado con el Real Madrid C. Así que el regreso de Enzo soluciona un problema y el jugador también tendrá vía libre para recuperar el terreno perdido en cuanto a minutos y competición tras un mes fuera de combate. Es una temporada importante para Enzo Alves, que tras dar el salto ya la pasada temporada al primer juvenil blanco, afronta la actual campaña como la de su consolidación en un filial estratégico de La Fábrica. Enzo tiene por delante una temporada ilusionante con el Real Madrid, con la Youth League como uno de los grandes escaparates, y también con la selección española, con la que, si todo va bien en las próximas semanas, disputará el Mundial sub 17 de Qatar, que arranca a finales de noviembre.

articles.title: La reacción de Arturo Vidal ante el 'caso Cristiano': "es una vergüenza"
articles.standfirst: El chileno critica el trato recibido por el portugués en su selección y también señala al cuerpo técnico por su gestión de la situación
articles.summary: El chileno critica el trato recibido por el portugués en su selección y también señala al cuerpo técnico por su gestión de la situación
articles.body: Las reacciones sobre lo que ha sucedido con Cristiano en la selección de Portugal no paran de llegar desde infinidades de rincones del planeta fútbol. A cada cual más razonable o antagónica, y en este último caso, incluso sorprendente. La última llega de alguien que podría parecer, cuando menos, inesperado, no por el personaje, sino por cómo ha sido su reacción: Arturo Vidal ha salido públicamente en defensa de Cristiano Ronaldo con unas contundentes declaraciones en las que lamenta el trato que, a su juicio, ha recibido el capitán portugués dentro de la selección. El centrocampista chileno no ocultó su malestar y aseguró que la gestión de la situación fue equivocada tanto desde el entorno del equipo nacional como desde el banquillo. “Muy feo lo que le hicieron en la selección y muy feo lo del técnico también”, afirmó Vidal, mostrando su respaldo a una de las grandes leyendas del fútbol mundial, y reconociendo que "es una vergüenza que un jugador que le ha dado todo a Portugual no puede salir así". Además, el jugador de Colo-Colo reivindicó la figura del cinco veces Balón de Oro y pidió un mayor reconocimiento a su trayectoria. “A Cristiano hay que cuidarlo, porque es uno de los mejores de la historia”, añadió. Las palabras de Vidal vuelven a poner el foco sobre el debate que suele acompañar a Cristiano Ronaldo en los últimos años de su carrera, especialmente en relación con su papel en la selección portuguesa. Para el chileno, sin embargo, el legado del delantero está fuera de toda discusión y merece un trato acorde a la dimensión de su figura. "Cristiano está en su derecho en hacer lo que quiera por ha llevado a su selección a otro nivel. Está entre los cuatro mejores jugadores de la historia".

articles.title: Cristiano y Leo en la hora del adiós
articles.standfirst: Ambas estrellas se mantienen fieles a sí mismas en sus últimos días sobre el césped
articles.summary: Ambas estrellas se mantienen fieles a sí mismas en sus últimos días sobre el césped
articles.body: La era de Cristiano y Messi ha terminado. En realidad acabó hace ya algún tiempo y lo que estamos viendo es uno de esos epílogos a tiempos de grandeza que a veces son dignos de ella y a veces no. Podría decirse que en el final cada uno está siendo fiel a sí mismo. Leo consume sus últimos días sobre el césped sin grandes estridencias fuera del mismo, porque los homenajes no lo son. Cristiano, intentando que nadie olvide quién es Cristiano Ronaldo. Así fue siempre y así es ahora. Ocioso es decir que la personalidad y las circunstancias de cada uno condicionarán, para algunos, su recuerdo -el fútbol es así, y por eso triunfa: por un sentido de pertenencia que bendice el sectarismo. Lo dijo el propio Santiago Bernabéu- pero tal cosa no será, ni mucho menos, justa, y en realidad hablará peor de quien lo haga que del personaje criticado. Ni a Cristiano le quita grandeza como jugador tener un carácter ostentóreo como dijo aquel presidente (carácter que otras estrellas del fútbol han tenido, que Di Stefano y Cruyff, por ejemplo, tenían su genio) ni al gran Barça de Messi y mucho menos a Messi se le puede descalificar citando a Negreira. Que es un hecho que debe tener su castigo -aunque si lo tiene, que está por ver, no será en España, donde Real Madrid y Barcelona están siempre a salvo de problemas graves, dado que el negocio descansa en ellos- pero cuya relación con la grandeza de Leo es irrelevante. Y eso, en realidad, lo saben hasta quienes la esgrimen. Así que ¿Qué nos queda? Pues disfrutar de lo que a ellos les quede. La carrera con el tiempo la tenemos todos perdida, así que disfrutemos del viaje de la mejor forma posible.

articles.summary: Los mejores equipos sub 13 del mundo se enfrentan en la X edición internacional del torneo en Estados Unidos
articles.body: Una Liga de ensueño. La FC Futures Internacional arranca su décima edición en Orlando, ciudad de fantasía por excelencia en los estados Unidos y en un recinto especial. La 'burbuja' (complejo ESPN Wide World of Sports, en Walt Disney World Resort) se abre de nuevo para que catorce de las mejores canteras del mundo pongan a prueba su nivel e intenten cargarse al sorprendente Elche que es el invitado de honor de esta décima edición al proclamarse campeón de la FC Futures de Villarreal derrotando a los grandes de LaLiga en un torneo perfecto. El actual campeón de la edición Internacional, el Atlético de Madrid, también desembarca como uno de los favoritos sin quitar ojo a equipos como el Real Madrid, el Betis o el Barcelona que nunca fallan en las últimas rondas. En el aspecto internacional los equipos más potentes son los brasileños de Palmeiras y Flamengo, aunque no se puede descartar a los argentinos River Plate y Boca que siempre compiten. El local Orlando y el mediático Inter Miami completaran un torneo dividido en cuatro grupos en el que se van a vivir emociones fuertes durante los próximos tres días. Por LaLiga FC Futures han pasado, siendo niños, Pau Cubarsí, Lamine Yamal o Gavi y otras leyendas históricas como Xavi Hernández, Iker Casillas, Andrés Iniesta, Fernando Torres, Gerard Piqué, Cesc Fàbregas y Santi Cazorla. Ese vínculo entre formación y élite es, precisamente, lo que LALIGA lleva más de una década exportando con este torneo. Para los clubes españoles supone medir su trabajo de cantera ante rivales de primer nivel internacional; para el aficionado estadounidense, una oportunidad poco habitual de ver de cerca cómo se forma un futbolista en España. articles.title: Ed Brand interview: Former Chelsea coach on his 17 years at Stamford Bridge and what he learned from the experience
articles.summary: In this exclusive interview with Sky Sports, Ed Brand discusses his journey with Chelsea from player to coach and what he has learned from his time in the academy, as a loan mentor, and with Swindon Town's first team. Now he is ready to be a head coach…
articles.body:
Brand was a player at Chelsea from the age of 10, captaining the youth team and playing for the reserves. An England under-17 international, his playing journey was curtailed in part by a series of concussions but he found a new passion in coaching.

He has coached FA Youth Cup winning teams at Chelsea, competed in Europe and worked with some of the best talents in English football. Now 39, he wants his departure to be the catalyst for the next step - and he has clear ideas about football.

Brand is a product of Chelsea in terms of how he sees the game, but the flexibility of that philosophy is interesting. It is about playing winning football. "I would not be happy if we had 73 per cent of the ball and lost without creating anything," he explains.

He knows the words that they want to hear at interview - and he can deliver that. "High-intensity football, with and without the ball, possession-based but with a purpose ." And yet, the lesson of his time at Chelsea was to help the players find their own solutions.

"I want to my teams to press with intensity but intelligence." That means players smelling the game for themselves sometimes too. "If football was that robotic, no one would watch it. You have got to have players who can make decisions," he argues.

"With the ball, I am not one of those coaches who says, 'this is my philosophy and I do not stray from it.' That is stubbornness. You should be stubborn around culture. But stubbornness around playing style? There are too many variables. The game changes.

"It all goes back to my Chelsea education. We had so many different ways of playing. If a team are going to give us 50 yards of space in behind, I do not want to take 15 passes to do what we could easily do in two. I want runners, especially if I have pace up top."

There is pride at the thought that he has played a small part in developing players who have proven themselves so adaptable. "Conor Gallagher can play anywhere in midfield. Reece James is another example. It is all because of their upbringing and exposure."

Brand continues: "Look at Marc Guehi. He played in midfield for Manchester City the other day. Again, that goes back to the education that he had within the academy, helping him to develop that ability to be able to play in different positions and systems."

But it was not just future England internationals like Guehi, Gallagher and James, like Lewis Hall and Tino Livramento, like Levi Colwill and Mason Mount who Brand worked with at Chelsea. Beyond the academy, he had two summers as a loan mentor as well.

Managing pre-season for those Chelsea players who were not in the first-team picture can be a challenge for a coach. For Brand, it was an opportunity. "It was brilliant for my education because I got to plan two eight-week pre-seasons with real senior players."

As a result, it tested the quality of his work but also his man-management skills. These were men who "might not be in the greatest head space" if their careers were not where they wanted them to me. "It was an eclectic group of personalities," says Brand.

He worked with Raheem Sterling and Romelu Lukaku, with Trevoh Chalobah and Ben Chilwell, those at the end and those at the beginning. "Some were excited for their first loan move, others had come back from loan and there were some about to be sold."

Brand acknowledges: "Most coaches would probably have looked at that situation from the outside and not wanted to touch it with a barge pole. I went the other way. These were Chelsea players, top players. They deserved the best pre-season they could get.

"I wanted those senior players to come away saying they loved it. It was a combination of staff taking it seriously, putting on really good sessions, and senior players buying into it and lifting the standard." Chalobah set the standards, Sterling drove the competition.

"Raheem was excellent. He wanted to win every time in training. Whatever the game you had to be on your toes as a coach. You had to make it competitive because he would pick up on everything. He is such a winner. Ben Chilwell, he was excellent too.

"It was not idyllic, it had its moments and it was a challenge logistically. We had no fixture list. No control of who comes in or goes out day to day. Suddenly players would leave and the numbers shrink. I would be lying if I said there were not difficult days.

"But over the course of a couple of months you could count those days on one hand and from a selfish point of view, it gave me another layer as a coach. You are not going to be walking into many circumstances that are potentially more difficult than that."

His time at Swindon Town might run it close. Brand tasted first-team coaching during what was ostensibly a secondment there as an assistant to Jody Morris. "It was massive for me. From a selfish perspective, I loved it. Jody let me lead on a lot of training."

He admits: "It was miles away from Chelsea." Not that being away from the comforts of Cobham was an issue. "My nature does not care about stuff like that. It was just about good people working hard. The players were great. It was a brilliant experience for me."

He talks of that period giving him "confidence and belief" that his ideas could translate. "I know I can go into a first-team environment and coach. If players think you don't know what you are talking about they find you out but it holds no apprehension now."

That Swindon dressing room was a mix. "Players forging their way and internationals who had played in the Premier League." But one conversation with the Wales international Jonny Williams helped to convince Brand that he had lots to contribute.

"No matter what job you do, if you work hard and show people you care, I have never known anybody not appreciate that. I remember going through clips with Jonny and he had not done that before. I could not believe it. This was a guy in his late 20s.

"It blows my mind that coaches do not do that stuff for players. Not only is it your job but if you think you are going through a season without a bad patch, you are naive. That is when, if you have credit in the bank, the team are going to get you out of it."

The plan now is to put these experiences of the past two decades into a new challenge. That could be at home or abroad but he wants what any coach wants, a project with clarity and prospects. "I will do my due diligence because they will be doing it on me."

He talks of "the importance of communication with the sporting director" and how "consistency in culture and behaviour is vital in leadership" but most of all it is just about getting back out onto the grass and putting all that knowledge into practice.

"I genuinely want to bounce out of bed looking forward to going into work and thinking about how I can influence things today. That is how my brain works," explains Brand. "I have done 17 years as a coach at Chelsea. Now I am ready for whatever comes next."

articles.body:
In Week 4, ESPN's College GameDay provided the preview for one of the biggest games of the season, a thrilling battle between Tennessee and Texas. This week, the program will head to Iowa for the first time in 20 years for another massive game.

Iowa, which pulled out a stunner over Michigan last week, will host the fifth-ranked Ohio State Buckeyes.

This will mark the first time this season that College GameDay won't be broadcast from an SEC site, though the reason is understandable. The crew will be ushering in one of the biggest Big Ten matchups of the year to date.

Crew: Rece Davis, alongside analysts Kirk Herbstreit, Desmond Howard, Pat McAfee, and Nick Saban

Iowa narrowly escaped Michigan last week, winning with a 16-yard walk-off touchdown pass from quarterback Hank Brown to wide receiver Reece Vander Zee. The Hawkeyes' victory was welcomed by College GameDay host Reece Davis.

"I root for the show, and it was going to be really, really good for the show if Iowa won on Saturday," Davis said on the College GameDay Podcast (h/t Qwame Skinner of Awful Announcing). "They did. And now, a big showdown with Ohio State coming up next week."

The showdown is indeed a big one. Iowa is one of four Big Ten teams entering Week 5 with a 4-0 record, while the 3-1 Buckeyes are looking to keep their path to the College Football Playoff open.

Ohio State's lone loss came against top-ranked Texas, which is why they haven't fallen far in the rankings.

This will mark the third time that Iowa has hosted College GameDay . All three occasions have preceded a battle with the Buckeyes.

In the game itself, Ohio State is fairly heavily favored, which shouldn't be a surprise. The Buckeyes have one of the most loaded teams in college football, as evidenced by the fact that they lost by a single point to the Longhorns in Austin.

Led by quarterback Julian Sayin and receiver Jeremiah Smith, Ohio State boasts one of the top offenses in the nation. However, they could face trouble at Kinnick Stadium.

Iowa will have the backing of a tremendous crowd, and their physical style of defense could make Sayin and Co. very uncomfortable early on. If the Hawkeyes can turn this into an ugly, methodical, physical game, they could force the kinds of mistakes that deliver another upset.

Let's not forget that the Buckeyes held a 23-3 lead against Texas going into the fourth quarter before collapsing on the road.

The prediction here is that Ohio State struggles early instead of late, but gets a late long drive from the offense and a couple of key defensive stops to pull away. Don't be surprised if this one is a lot closer than many seem to expect.

articles.title: Dev's Digest: Hamza Choudhury's FA Cup final shirt up for grabs, award-winning pair stand with Zidane Iqbal, Dilan Markanday opens up on wonder-goal
articles.summary: Also in Dev's Digest, the column that sets the record straight on British South Asians in The Game: Asian Football Award winners stand with Zidane Iqbal; Dilan Markanday opens up on Chesterfield wonder-goal ahead of Saturday's visit of Tranmere, live on Sky Sports Football
articles.body:
Hamza Choudhury's shirt from Leicester City's 2021 FA Cup final win against Chelsea will be auctioned for charity later this month, Sky Sports News can exclusively reveal.

The framed shirt will be auctioned at a fundraiser for the Children Not Numbers charity, in aid of children affected by the conflict in Gaza, organised by Muslim athlete representation body Nujum Sports.

Choudhury, who ended his 21-year association with Leicester to join Sheffield United over the summer, will be speaking at the event in London on October 25.

Choudhury has been in action at the ASEAN Cup where Fulham youngster Farhaan Ali Wahid followed in his footsteps and made his international debut, becoming only the second Premier League footballer in history to play for the Bangladesh national team.

Ali Wahid, who is currently on loan at National League leaders Boreham Wood, came off the bench and scored on his second Bangladesh appearance in Thursday's defeat to Indonesia.

Elsewhere, Oxford City winger Dillon De Silva was on target for Sri Lanka in a 3-0 victory against Seychelles, before scoring again in a 2-0 win against the same opposition in the international double-header between the two sides on Mahe Island.

Benning and Kandola: Players stand with 'great example' Iqbal

Mal Benning and Kam Kandola say Britain's South Asian heritage footballers stand with Zidane Iqbal after the Dundee United midfielder was targeted while on international duty with Iraq.

Manchester-born Iqbal bravely spoke out, telling reporters last weekend he had been subjected to verbal and online abuse because his father is British-Pakistani.

Iqbal was unable to accept his Men's Player award at the Asian Football Awards - where Benning was also being recognised with the Football Pioneer award as exclusively revealed in last month's edition of Dev's Digest.

Ahead of the ceremony, Benning, who has made four consecutive appearances in the South Asians in Football Team of the Season , told Sky Sports News: "For him to experience that abuse is saddening.

"I'm saddened by it, because Zidane Iqbal is a great example for South Asians playing football - he's played at the World Cup.

"Hopefully, this is a one-off for Zidane and it doesn't put a dampener on any South Asian looking up and trying to be a professional footballer.

"All we can do as a community is stick together and make sure we're there for Zidane. I know the young lad, he's done well for himself.

"Hopefully, he'll have a great career. I'm saddened, but we're all here for him, definitely."

Hereford's Kam Kandola, who picked up the Non-League Player award, said he was proud of Iqbal for taking a stand for South Asians in the game.

"We all stand by him and it's important that he is proud of his heritage," Kandola told Sky Sports News.

"I'm proud of him if anything. It's a difficult situation. Some people shy away from it but he stood up to it - and for himself and his heritage.

"I'm quite impressed [by how he handled it]. We all stand by him."

Wrexham and Pakistan forward Mariam Mahmood won the Women's Player accolade at the Asian Football Awards.

Her international team-mate, Lewes midfielder Layla Banaras, landed the Women's Young Player award.

Khela excited about potential Savage appointment

Brandon Khela has admitted the prospect of Robbie Savage becoming the next Peterborough United manager is an exciting one.

Forest Green Rovers chairman Dale Vince said in a statement this week that Savage has been offered the Peterborough job, with the two clubs negotiating terms.

Ex-Birmingham City midfielder Khela, who scooped the Men's Young Player accolade at the Asian Football Awards, thinks he could learn a lot from Savage who was once a cult figure at St Andrew's himself as a player.

"He has played in the Premier League, the highest level, which I aspire to get to," Khela told Sky Sports News .

"I could definitely learn a lot from him, if it is him. Whatever manager comes in, it doesn't matter who it is, I'm just looking forward to whoever is coming in. I'm really excited for that.

"I've still got loads to improve on in my game, and if it is him, I hope to learn a lot from him."

Former England youth international Khela was also full of praise for Luke Williams following his dismissal as Peterborough manager a fortnight ago.

"I have a lot of good things to say about Luke," Khela said.

"I learnt a lot from him, but that's football I guess and I hope our paths cross again in the future."

Markanday: My eyes lit up when I got 1v1

Trailblazer Dilan Markanday said his solo stunner for Chesterfield earlier this month made him feel like the fearless kid who was once arguably Tottenham's best academy prospect.

Markanday, who became the first British South Asian to play for Tottenham Hotspur in 140 years of club history when he featured in a European game under Nuno Espirito Santo five years ago, rounded off the scoring in style in a recent 2-0 win for the Spireites against York City.

Ahead of Chesterfield's early-season six-pointer against Tranmere, live on Sky Sports Football at lunchtime on Saturday, Markanday explained how the goal was the kind he would score for fun when he was coming through at Spurs.

"I think it was in the 96th, 97th minute, it was late in the game, and I still had the fuel and the energy to keep going" Markanday told Sky Sports News.

"When that ball came to me on the halfway line, I think a lot of fans and even the gaffer was saying go down the line and just hold it in the corner, because we were up 1-0.

"I disregarded that, which ended up paying off, and my eyes lit up as soon as I got one-vs-one with the defender - that's the situation I want to be in. I managed to get past him, and took on another player and hit it into the bottom corner. I was absolutely ecstatic when it went in.

"I actually felt like that sort of little kid again back at Tottenham, you know taking on players - and that's what has allowed me to have the career I've had. I felt really good in that moment.

"I just want to keep continuing to score goals, different types of goals and just enjoy my football with that 'childlike kid in a playground' sort of feeling where there's no fear, there's nothing to prove to anyone, just going out there and enjoying your football.

"I've just got to remember that and play with no fear. I was just happy with the goal and hopefully they keep coming."

For more stories, features and videos, visit our ground-breaking South Asians in football page on skysports.com and get in touch with us here to have your say.
